Rueda
RWAY-dah
n. (the Aragonese Cistercian abbey of 1182, named for the great waterwheel that raised the Ebro into its cloister)
Spanish rueda, a wheel, for the abbey's water-wheel on the Ebro.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Rueda de Ebro in Aragon was founded in 1182 by Alfonso II and settled from Escaladieu by way of Junéria, and it took its name from the engineering that made it possible: a great undershot water-wheel in the Ebro, turned by the current, which raised river water into a channel feeding the abbey's fountain, kitchen, fishpond and irrigated gardens. The wheel has been reconstructed. The abbey was suppressed in 1835 and the buildings are now a hotel and a monument. The dictionary records Rueda for the wheel, because lifting water uphill is a figure Scripture uses for the one thing men cannot do for themselves. The prophet's charge against a people is that they left a spring and dug tanks, “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns” (Jer 2:13). The river that gladdens the city is not pumped, “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Psa 46:4). The tree the prophet blesses is near water rather than supplied with it, “For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters” (Jer 17:8), and the question put to all such labour concerns what it is buying, “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” (Isa 55:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a noria would be a water-wheel for raising water; a cistern as a receptacle for water; a conduit as a channel for conveying water; irrigation as the watering of land; and a fountain as a spring.

expand to see more

WHEEL, n. A circular frame turning on an axis; a machine for raising water.

CISTERN, n. An artificial reservoir or receptacle for holding water, beer or other liquor.

CONDUIT, n. A canal or pipe for the conveyance of water; a duct.

IRRIGATION, n. The act of watering or moistening; the operation of causing water to flow over lands.

FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; the source or head of a stream.

Key Scripture

Jer 2:13 — "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water."

Psa 46:4 — "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High."

Jer 17:8 — "For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit."

Isa 55:2 — "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness."

Modern Corruption

Aragonese Cistercian abbey of 1182 whose great Ebro water-wheel raised the river into its cloister.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that living water comes from a spring and not from a wheel. Rueda raised the Ebro into its own fountain by the force of the current, honest ingenuity of a kind the order excelled at, and the prophet's charge against a people is framed in exactly that contrast, “For my people have committed two evils” (Jer 2:13).

The live temptation is the cistern, which is to substitute a contrivance of one's own making for a supply one did not make. The river that gladdens the city is simply there, “the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High” (Psa 46:4); the blessed tree is near water rather than irrigated, “and that spreadeth out her roots by the river” (Jer 17:8); and the question put to the whole enterprise is about what it buys, “and your labour for that which satisfieth not?” (Isa 55:2).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maqor (H4726), a spring; Hebrew bor (H0877), a cistern; Hebrew nahar (H5104), a river; Hebrew shoresh (H8328), a root.

expand to see more

Hebrew maqor (H4726) — a spring, a fountain; “the fountain of living waters”, Jeremiah 2:13.

Hebrew bor (H0877) — a cistern, a pit, a well; “broken cisterns, that can hold no water”, Jeremiah 2:13.

Hebrew nahar (H5104) — a river, a stream; “There is a river”, Psalm 46:4.

Hebrew shoresh (H8328) — a root; “that spreadeth out her roots by the river”, Jeremiah 17:8.

Hebrew sabea (H7646) — to be sated, to be satisfied; “for that which satisfieth not?”, Isaiah 55:2.

Usage

"“the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13) — a spring, not a wheel."

"“There is a river” (Psa 46:4) — simply there, not pumped."

"“as a tree planted by the waters” (Jer 17:8) — near water rather than irrigated."
